_comment: Three tiles, and the point of the third is CONCURRENCY, not coverage. The shipped two-tile cut holds both EfficientNet-b0 encoders in one graph, so they serialise inside a single dispatch on one lane. They do not consume each other's output -- the goal encoder takes goal_img plus obs_img, the obs encoder takes obs_img -- so branch-mode slicing (backward closure of each compress projection) makes them independent tiles with depends_on: []. Measured, one lane per machine kind: goal encoder on CPU int8 (6.615 ms) overlapping the obs encoder on DSP (9.533 ms), then the transformer on CPU fp32 (13.559 ms) = 23.955 ms makespan, against 29.379 ms for the shipped two-tile set. The extra dispatch the split costs is exactly what the overhead model predicts: the same three tiles run end-to-end with no concurrency are 29.764 ms, i.e. +0.385 ms over the two-tile 29.379 ms against a predicted 0.367 ms DSP dispatch + 5.4 ns x 512 boundary bytes. So the split pays for itself 15x over. The decoder's op range is not a single span because ops 0-5 and 1070 are constant subgraphs shared by every tile that needs them.

_provenance.statistic: median of per-sweep median_us, performance governor, CPU cells unmasked
_provenance.op_index_space: flow_c IR (605 ops, pytorch_export:vint) -- derived by qnn_models/slicing_study/ir_branch_ranges.py, the same backward-closure partition the ONNX slicer runs, applied to the IR's depends_on edges. The two encoders have NO shared ancestor in IR space, so the partition is exactly ops 0-295 / 296-538 / 539-604. Each binding also carries _ops_onnx_nodes, the node ranges of the ONNX the artifacts were actually sliced from (1931 nodes); the two spaces differ, as they do for yolov8n.
